title: Rotated Digits
statement:
Turning a single digit upside down (a 180 degree rotation) behaves like this: `0`, `1` and `8` stay the same, `2` and `5` turn into each other, `6` and `9` turn into each other, and `3`, `4` and `7` stop being digits at all.

Call a positive integer **good** when turning every one of its digits in place (no digit may be skipped) leaves only digits, and the number they spell differs from the original. Return how many good integers lie between `1` and `n`, both ends included.
notes:
## Intuition

With `n` at most `10^4`, simply looking at every number from `1` to `n` is fast enough. Each number only needs two facts about its digits: does it contain a digit that cannot be turned (`3`, `4`, `7`), and does it contain at least one digit that turns into a *different* digit (`2`, `5`, `6`, `9`)? A number is good exactly when the first answer is no and the second is yes. Digits `0`, `1` and `8` are harmless but never make the number change on their own. (A digit DP over the decimal string reaches O(log n), but enumeration is the clearer idea at this size.)

## Approach

1. Keep `count` of good numbers, and loop `x` from `1` to `n`.
2. Copy `x` into `value`, start with `valid = true` and `changed = false`.
3. Peel off the last digit with `value % 10` while `value > 0` and the number is still valid.
4. A `3`, `4` or `7` makes it invalid; a `2`, `5`, `6` or `9` sets `changed`.
5. Drop that digit with `Math.floor(value / 10)`.
6. If `valid && changed`, add one to `count`. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 10`. For `x = 1` the only digit is `1`: valid but unchanged, so not good. `x = 2` sets `changed`, so `count = 1`. `x = 3` and `x = 4` are invalid. `x = 5` and `x = 6` are good (`count = 3`), `x = 7` is invalid, `x = 8` is unchanged, `x = 9` is good (`count = 4`). For `x = 10` the digits `0` and `1` are both unchanged, so the answer stays `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): each of the `n` numbers has about log₁₀ n digits.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters and flags.

## Pitfalls

- A number made only of `0`, `1` and `8` (like `1`, `10`, `88`) is valid but not good, because it does not change.
- One bad digit anywhere ruins the whole number; do not stop at the first changing digit.
- The range starts at `1`, not `0`, and includes `n` itself.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | good numbers found so far |
| `x` | the number being examined |
| `value` | what is left of `x` as its digits are removed |
| `valid` | no digit seen so far is `3`, `4` or `7` |
| `changed` | some digit seen so far turns into a different digit |
| `digit` | the current last digit of `value` |

narration.2: The tally of good numbers starts at zero.
narration.4: Enumerate every candidate from 1 up to and including n.
narration.5: Work on a copy so x itself stays intact for the loop.
narration.6: Assume the number can be rotated until a bad digit shows up.
narration.7: No digit that changes on rotation has been seen yet.
narration.9: Look at digits one by one from the right, stopping early once the number is ruined.
narration.10: The last decimal digit of what remains.
narration.11: 3, 4 and 7 are not digits after rotation...
narration.13: 2, 5, 6 and 9 turn into a different digit...
narration.14: ...so the rotated number will differ from x.
narration.19: Good means every digit rotates and at least one of them changes.
narration.23: Every number in [1, n] has been examined; return the tally.
